sentences.text: The largest species, Mosasaurus hoffmanni, is estimated to reach a maximum length of 12 meters.

Hermann Schlegel demonstrated in 1854 that Mosasaurus possessed fully aquatic flippers rather than limbs for walking. These flippers are broad, flat, and shaped like paddles used for steering underwater.
Schlegel also demonstrated that Mosasaurus phalanges lacked muscle or tendon attachments, making walking impossible.
Experts believe Mosasaurus lived near the ocean surface, where it fed on fish, turtles, ammonites, and possibly smaller mosasaurs.

The first fossils of Mosasaurus were discovered as skulls in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in the late 18th century. One skull discovered in 1778 was nicknamed the "great animal of Maastricht".

A second skull was found in the same quarry in 1778, which attracted the attention of Johann Leonard Hoffmann. The first known Mosasaurus fossil, cataloged as TM 7424, is currently displayed at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.
Derived mosasaurs like Mosasaurus are now understood to have builds similar to ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales due to convergent evolution.
The genus Mosasaurus was named by William Daniel Conybeare in 1822. The type species of the genus Mosasaurus is Mosasaurus hoffmanni.
Species described within the genus Mosasaurus include M. missouriensis, M. conodon, M. lemonnieri, and M. beaugei.
Mosasaurus is the type genus of the family Mosasauridae and subfamily Mosasaurinae, and belongs to the order Squamata.
Mosasaurus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian). Mosasaurus lived between 70 and 66 million years ago.

Mosasaurus fossils have been found in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Western Asia, and Antarctica. Mosasaurus inhabited areas of modern Western Europe, North America, South America, and Antarctica.
Scientists continue to debate whether the closest living relatives of Mosasaurus are monitor lizards or snakes.
An unclear diagnosis of the type species M. hoffmanni led to historically problematic classification issues.

The taxonomic validity of M. lemonnieri has been the subject of long-standing debate. In 2004, Mulder, Cornelissen, and Verding suggested that M. lemonnieri might be a juvenile form of M. hoffmanni, a hypothesis contested by later anatomical studies.
